title: Cap. 4 Mem. 3: Abelard objection on eternal decree — Halensis/Aquinas/Scripture/Augustine
pass_a_gloss: Obj.2 (greater scruple): God from eternity not only foreknew but predestined to whom he will infallibly give faith/remissio/eternal life, to whom not; God cannot in time act otherwise than he eternally foreknew/decreed. Abelard boldly: God can do nothing beyond what he did or will do. If so, since for most God neither foreknew nor decreed producing faith in them, faith-condition in no way possible for non-elect still in this life. Sol.: True God does/permits nothing without antecedent eternal decree & foreknowledge. False that he cannot by ordinary power do anything beyond what he foreknew/decreed to do. Halensis 1.21.4.2: Divine power not limited by will or foreknowledge, though egress into act always accompanied by them. Aquinas: doing subject to maker’s foreknowledge/ordination; being-able is natural — God does because he wills, but can not because he wills but because powerful by nature (1.25.5 ad1). De Potentia art.5 ad1: ‘God can do only what he foreknows he will do’ double — if NISI to power (POTEST) false (can do more than he foreknows he will); if to act (FACERE) true (nothing done by God not foreknown) but that sense irrelevant. Some so absorb secret eternal will/foreknowledge they admit almost nothing else — show briefly Scripture, Fathers, reason forbid settling what is possible/impossible to God by ordinary power according to secret eternal predestination decrees. Scriptures: do not restrict power by secret decrees but extend by infinite strength & revealed word-rule. Matt 3:9 stones→Abraham’s children; 19:26 all possible with God; 26:53 twelve legions; Mark 14:36 all possible transfer cup; Rom 11:23 can re-graft Jews; 14:4 God able to make stand; 2 Cor 9:8 able to make all grace abound. So do not judge power from secret decrees — he did not decree those examples, indeed decreed/foreknew he would not do them, yet Scriptures do not call them impossible. Augustine: Almighty can do many things he neither wills nor does. On Judas (undisputed reprobate): Lord who raised Lazarus in body — could he not raise Judas in mind? He could, but would not. Affirm same of any viator despite secret will/foreknowledge: God can raise any in mind = give penitence/faith/saving grace — revealed of none that he wills not this, of each that by ordinary power he can while still on the way. Cling to this revealed will; do not divine possibility from utterly unknown will.
pass_b_english: That also is objected which seems to cast a greater scruple: that God from eternity not only foreknew but predestined to whom he will infallibly give faith, remission, and eternal life, and to whom he will not: But God cannot in time act otherwise, or otherwise than he from eternity foreknew and decreed that he would do. On this argument Abelard once boldly asserted that God cannot do anything beyond those things which he has done or is going to do. If this holds, since it is certain that as to the greater part of human beings God neither foreknew faith to be produced in them nor decreed it, there is no ground for our saying that this condition of faith is in any way possible as to the non-elect still constituted in this life.

That God does or permits nothing without an antecedent eternal decree and eternal foreknowledge is most true. But if anyone thence concludes that God cannot do by ordinary power anything beyond those things which he foreknew and decreed to be done, that is most false. For as our Halensis rightly has it, Part 1, question 21, article 4, member 2: Divine power is limited neither by God’s will nor by his foreknowledge, although the egress of Divine power into act is always accompanied by his foreknowledge and will. Aquinas renders a reason of this matter fit enough, namely: Because the very doing is subject to the foreknowledge and ordination of the one doing; but not the very being-able, which is natural. For God therefore does something because he wills; yet he can not therefore because he wills, but because he is powerful by his nature (Part 1, question 25, article 5, to the first). The same Aquinas answers the aforesaid objection in form in the Disputed Questions On the Power of God, article 5, reply to 1, whose words I will set down: This locution, God CANNOT DO EXCEPT WHAT HE FOREKNOWS HE WILL DO, is twofold: because the exceptive particle EXCEPT is referred either to the power which is imported by the verb CAN, or to the act which is imported by the verb DO. If in the first way, then the locution is false: For God can do more things than he foreknows he will do. If in the second way, then the sense is that it cannot be that something is done by God and is not foreknown by God: so the locution is true; but this sense does nothing for the purpose. Thus far he. But because some so wholly lean on this contemplation of the eternal and secret will and foreknowledge that they admit almost nothing else into their minds, we will show briefly that neither the Scriptures, nor the Fathers, nor reason itself permit that according to these secret and eternal decrees of predestination it be established by us what is possible for God, or impossible, according to his ordinary power.

Let us begin from the Scriptures: which are accustomed not to restrict God’s power according to the secret decrees of his will, but to extend it according to God’s infinite strength, and according to the rule revealed in the word. ([[Matthew 3:9 >> Bible:Matthew 3:9]]): God is able from these stones to raise up children of Abraham. ([[Matthew 19:26 >> Bible:Matthew 19:26]]): All things are possible with God. And ([[Matthew 26:53 >> Bible:Matthew 26:53]]): Can I not ask the Father, and he will exhibit to me more than twelve legions of angels? ([[Mark 14:36 >> Bible:Mark 14:36]]): All things are possible to you: transfer this cup from me. So also the Apostle speaks of the refractory Jews: God is able to graft them in again ([[Romans 11:23 >> Bible:Romans 11:23]]). And of any fallen human being: Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own Lord he stands or falls. But he will stand: for God is able to make him stand ([[Romans 14:4 >> Bible:Romans 14:4]]). Finally of any wayfarer that is true: God is able to make all grace abound in him ([[2 Corinthians 9:8 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 9:8]]). I pass over more. From these it is plain enough that God’s power is least to be judged from his secret decrees: For he did not decree to raise children of Abraham from stones, nor to free Christ from the Jews’ hands, nor to raise and establish any fallen person, nor to pour the abundance of his grace into any and all: indeed he decreed and foreknew that he would least do all these things, which yet (if we are willing to hear the sacred Scriptures) are not therefore held for impossibles.

Augustine to this sense: Almighty God can do many things which he neither wills nor does. The same Father also presses the point in Judas himself, a reprobate beyond controversy: The Lord, he says, who raised Lazarus in the body — could he not raise Judas in the mind? He could indeed, but he was unwilling. What Augustine does not fear to affirm of Judas, let us intrepidly affirm of any wayfarer, the secret will or foreknowledge of God concerning the same notwithstanding: namely that God can raise anyone in the mind, that is, gift him with penitence and faith and saving grace; because of no particular human being has he revealed that he wills not this, and of each he has revealed that by ordinary power he can do this while he is still constituted on the way. On this will we ought to lean, and least to divine about the possibility or impossibility of things from a will utterly unknown to us.
source_text:
Objicitur et illud, quod majorem scrupulum videtur injicere, Deum ab aeterno non solum praescivisse sed praedestinasse quibus infallibiliter daturus est fidem, remissionem et vitam aeternam, quibus non daturus: Non potest autem Deus in tempore alia aut aliter agere quam ab aeterno praescivit et decrevit se facturum. Hoc argumento olim nixus Abailardus audacter asseruit, Deum non posse aliquid facere praeter ea quae fecit aut facturus est. Si hoc obtineat, cum certum sit quoad majorem hominum partem Deum nec praescivisse fidem in illis producendam, nec decrevisse, non est quod dicamus hanc fidei conditionem esse ullo modo possibilem quoad non-electos in hac vita etiamnum constitutos.

Deum absque aeterno decreto et aeterna praescientia antecedente nihil agere aut permittere, verissimum est. Sed si quis inde concludat Deum non posse facere juxta potentiam ordinariam quicquam praeter ea quae praescivit et decrevit facienda, falsissimum est. Nam ut recte Halensis noster, Part. 1. qu. 21. art. 4. memb. 2, Divina potentia nec voluntate nec praescientia Dei limitatur, quamvis egressum Divinae potentiae in actum semper praescientia ejus et voluntas concomitetur. Rationem hujus rei satis idoneam reddit Aquinas, nempe, Quia ipsum facere subjacet praescientiae et ordinationi facientis; non autem ipsum posse quod est naturale. Ideo enim Deus aliquid facit quia vult, non tamen ideo potest quia vult, sed quia potens est natura sua, Part. 1. qu. 25. art. 5. ad 1. Idem Aquinas praedictae objectioni in forma respondet, Quaest. Disp. De Potentia Dei art. 5. Resp. ad 1, cujus verba apponam, Haec locutio, Deus NON POTEST FACERE NISI QUOD PRAESCIT SE FACTURUM, est duplex: quia particula exceptiva NISI refertur vel ad potentiam quae importatur per verbum POTEST, vel ad actum qui importatur per verbum FACERE. Si primo modo, tunc locutio est falsa: Plura enim potest facere Deus quam praesciat se facturum. Si secundo modo, tum sensus est, quod non potest esse quod aliquid fiat a Deo, et non sit a Deo praescitum: sic locutio est vera; sed hic sensus nihil facit ad propositum. Hactenus ille. Verum quia nonnulli ita toti incumbunt huic aeternae et arcanae voluntatis praescientiaeque contemplationi, ut nihil fere aliud in animos suos admittant, ostendemus breviter, neque Scripturas, neque Patres, neque ipsam rationem permittere ut secundum arcana haec et aeterna decreta praedestinationis statuatur a nobis quid possibile sit Deo, aut impossibile secundum ordinariam ejus potentiam.

Ordiamur a Scripturis: quae non artare solent Dei potentiam secundum arcana decreta voluntatis ejus, sed eam extendere secundum infinitas Dei vires, et secundum regulam in verbo revelatam. Matth. iii. 9, Potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae. Matth. xix. 26, Omnia possibilia sunt apud Deum. Et Matth. xxvi. 53, An non possum rogare Patrem, et exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones angelorum? Marc. xiv. 36, Omnia tibi possibilia sunt: transfer calicem hunc a me. Sic etiam loquitur Apostolus, de Judaeis refractariis, Potens est Deus iterum inserere illos, Rom. xi. 23. Et de quovis homine lapso, Tu quis es qui judicas alienum servum? Domino suo stat aut cadit. Stabit autem: Potens est enim Deus statuere eum, Rom. xiv. 4. denique de quolibet viatore Verum est illud, Potens est Deus omnem gratiam abundare facere in eo, 2 Cor. ix. 8. Pluribus supersedeo. Ex hisce satis liquet, de potentia Dei ex arcanis ejus decretis minime esse judicandum: Non enim decrevit ex lapidibus excitare filios Abrahae, non Christum liberare e manibus Judaeorum, non quemvis lapsum erigere et statuminare, non gratiae suae copiam in quosvis effundere: imo decrevit et praescivit se haec omnia minime facturum, quae tamen (si sacras Scripturas audire velimus) non idcirco pro impossibilibus habentur.

Augustinus in hanc sententiam, Omnipotens Deus multa potest facere quae nec vult nec facit. Instat etiam idem Pater in ipso Juda, extra controversiam reprobo, Dominus, inquit, qui Lazarum suscitavit in corpore, non potuit Judam suscitare in mente? Potuit quidem, sed noluit. Quod de Juda non veretur affirmare Augustinus, id nos de quovis viatore intrepide affirmemus, non obstante arcana Dei voluntate aut praescientia de eodem, nempe posse Deum quemvis in mente suscitare, id est, poenitentia et fide ac gratia salutifera donare; quia de nullo particulari homine revelavit se hoc nolle, et de quolibet revelavit se per potentiam ordinariam hoc posse facere, dum est in via adhuc constitutus. Huic voluntati nos oportet incumbere, et de possibilitate aut impossibilitate rerum ex voluntate nobis prorsus incognita minime hariolari.
